sentences.t: I'm in my final year of med school, and during a normal exam block I study about six hours a day.
People always ask how I don't burn out, and the honest answer is I did burn out, badly, in second year.
So everything in this video is stuff I changed after that.
Number one, I stopped studying in one giant block.
I do four ninety-minute sessions with real breaks in between, like leave-the-room breaks, not phone-on-the-couch breaks.
Ninety minutes is about how long I can actually focus before my brain starts reading the same sentence four times.
Number two, I plan the day the night before, in about five minutes.
And this is where my whole system lives now.
All of my notes and my study plan are in Notewell.
It's a notes app, but it's built for studying, so you can turn any highlight into a flashcard with one tap.
Then it schedules your reviews for you with spaced repetition, so you see the cards you're about to forget, not the ones you already know.
I have every lecture from this year in there, and when I search for something like heart failure drugs, it pulls up every note and card across all my courses.
It works offline, which matters, because the library basement here has zero signal.
You can try it for free, and if you go to notewell.app slash hana you get two months of the premium plan on me.
That link is in the description.
Okay, number three, and this one sounds silly.
I eat lunch away from my desk, no textbook, no podcast about cardiology.
For about two years I ate over my notes and told myself it was efficient.
It wasn't, I just got crumbs in my notes and a headache by three p.m.
Number four, I protect my sleep like it's an exam.
Seven and a half hours minimum, same wake-up time every day, even on weekends.
I know that sounds boring.
But when I tracked my practice scores against my sleep last year, the difference was honestly kind of embarrassing.
On nights under six hours, my scores the next day dropped by about ten percent.
Number five, active recall over rereading, every single time.
Rereading feels productive because it's comfortable.
Closing the book and trying to explain the topic out loud to an empty room is uncomfortable, and that's exactly why it works.
I literally talk to my plant.
His name is Gerald, and he knows a lot about renal physiology at this point.
Number six, I schedule one full day off every week.
Not a half day where I feel guilty, a full day where I don't open anything.
That one was the hardest to accept, and it's also the one that fixed my burnout the most.
And last, I stopped comparing my hours to other people's.
Somebody on the internet will always be studying twelve hours a day.
Good for them, I'd be crying in a stairwell.
Find the amount you can keep up for months, not days.
So that's my system right now.
If you want a full video on how I make my flashcards, let me know below.
And good luck with whatever you're studying for, you've got this.
